title: Stewardship of creation (CCC 2415–2418)
hook: animals and the earth entrusted to our care

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh commandment: don't steal, pay what's fair, share what the earth gives. Your line was goods are for all.

A sister leaves for two weeks of work and hands over a leash and a watering can. Walk the dog morning and night; water the balcony plants every other day. The dog isn't the sitter's, and neither are the plants. But for two weeks, whether they thrive is up to the one holding the leash. A good sitter checks the soil with a finger, notices if the dog stops eating, and never treats the spare key as permission for anything. The Catechism files this under the seventh commandment.
screen: `A LEASH AND A WATERING CAN.` → `THE DOG IS NOT YOURS.` → `TWO WEEKS IN YOUR CARE.`

segments.voice: Year one called creation very good. Now, our part in it. Genesis tells how God placed the man in paradise, in the Douay-Rheims, "to dress it, and to keep it." Two jobs: work it, and guard it. Beside it, the earlier line about dominion, ruling over the fish and the birds, sounds different. Dominion, the Catechism says, is not absolute. It's limited by concern for our neighbors, including the people who come after us, and it asks for a religious respect for the integrity of creation. A steward is the one holding the leash: not the owner, the one entrusted. Then the animals. They are God's creatures, the Catechism says; he surrounds them with his providential care, and by simply being, they bless him and give him glory. So people owe them kindness, as saints like Francis of Assisi and Philip Neri showed. Proverbs puts it in one line: "The just regardeth the lives of his beasts." The hard edges, said plainly: animals may be used for food and clothing, and medical experiments on them are acceptable within reasonable limits, if they help to care for or save human lives. But it is contrary to human dignity to cause animals to suffer or die needlessly. And a balance: it's right to love animals, but not to give them the love owed only to persons, and money spent on them shouldn't come first when people are in need. Stewardship holds two hands open: one for the creature in front of you, one for the neighbor you haven't met yet.
screen: `TO DRESS IT, AND TO KEEP IT.` · `DOMINION IS NOT ABSOLUTE.` · `ANIMALS GIVE GOD GLORY.` · `NO NEEDLESS SUFFERING.`

segments.voice: If there's an animal or a plant near you, a plant on the windowsill, go to it now; if not, bring one to mind. Look at it as something entrusted, not owned, and ask what it needs today: water, a walk, a little shade, a clean bowl. If you pray, thank God for this one small creature; if you don't, just keep it company a while.
Stewardship. Caring for what belongs to another: in Catholic teaching, the earth and its creatures, held in trust for God and for the neighbors who come after us. Today's word.
Your line: entrusted. The earth is held in trust for God and those to come. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Catechism treats care for creation as part of the seventh commandment; some parishes bless animals on the feast of Saint Francis of Assisi, and some families teach children to care for pets and gardens as a duty to God.

fork.setup: you're looking after a sister's dog and plants for two weeks. the Catechism's word for your job is stewardship. which is closest?
options: they're yours to do with as you like.
you keep them well, for someone else.
you leave them alone and touch nothing.
fork.reveal: a steward is entrusted, not the owner. the Catechism says dominion over creation is not absolute; it's care, limited by concern for neighbors and those who come after.

original.note: Hebrew: to keep, to guard, to watch over — the verb behind "to keep it" in Genesis 2:15.

trapdoor: what you thought: dominion means the earth is ours to use up.
what it means: the earth and its creatures are entrusted to us, to work and to keep, with care for neighbors to come.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:15 gives two verbs, to work and to keep; the Catechism says dominion is limited by care for neighbors and for the generations to come.

chat.says: If God gave people dominion over animals, can we treat them however we want?
options: No. The Catechism says dominion isn't absolute; animals give God glory, and needless suffering is wrong.
Yes. Animals have no worth of their own, so any use of them at all is fine in Catholic teaching.
Yes, as long as the animal belongs to you; only harming someone else's animal is wrong.
chat.meaning: Dominion is limited by care for neighbors and those to come. Animals bless God by being, and causing them needless suffering offends human dignity.
